evidence: Draft judged: “Is this way of responding helping you to be clearer and steadier and less hooked?” It replaces “The useful question is whether this way of responding helps you become clearer, steadier, and less hooked.” and appears once in CONTEXT.txt, as the last line of the fourth paragraph of the section headed “A response check, not a verdict about what it is”, after “You don’t have to find out if it’s a guard immediately, and you may not be able to comfort it quickly.” It does what the_change says: Emulate's question with his “this way of responding” where Emulate had “it”. That swap matters: in this section “it” is always the inner part (“what it is”, “if it’s a guard”, “comfort it”), so “Is it helping you…” would have asked about the part and not about the response; the draft asks about the response, which is the published test. MEANING: same test, same three outcomes in his order (clearer, steadier, less hooked), nothing added. What is lost is the announcing frame “The useful question is”, which also marked this as the question to ask instead of a verdict; the heading (“A response check, not a verdict about what it is”), “you don’t have to know what it is” two paragraphs up and the sentence before it carry that contrast, so the point survives. “helps you become” (general) to “is helping you to be” (right now) suits a check done in the middle of the practice and is not a different test. READ IN CONTEXT: I read the whole section, then the line. “this way of responding” points back to the responses the section has just given (warm or arm's length, the boundary, the Nurturer, stopping, comforting) and to the heading's “response”, so C02 is clean. The question reads as speech, follows the reassurance before it without a seam, and ends the section on the check the heading promises rather than on a flourish. No space before the question mark and no stray quote marks. TELL ROWS: T01, T03 to T08, T11, T16, T18, T23, T25, T27 ABSENT (no first-person stake, scene, prop, filler, image-plus-explanation, bridge, contrast, premise-and-flip, scenery, colon reveal or tic word). T02: the first three paragraphs of the section are a run of second-person instructions, but that cadence is in the unchanged text; the draft takes the slot of the sentence it replaces, adds no job, and drops an announcing frame, so it does not add to it. T06 ABSENT (clearer, steadier, less hooked are his published criteria, not vague healing language). T09 and T13 (the D9 pointers) ABSENT: one question with its reason in the sentence before; nothing added or removed in the paragraph. T10 ABSENT. T12 ABSENT: the three outcomes are his published three, a short test, not a taxonomy; the “and … and” loosens the comma triad the source had. T14 and T15 ABSENT: nothing moved; the words are his (“this way of responding”, “clearer”, “steadier”, “less hooked”) and the sentence changed form (statement to question), so it is not a swap of words with the structure left standing. T17 ABSENT. T19 improved: the announcing frame is gone. T20 ABSENT: the last line is the section's named check, a plain question with no twist or antithesis. T21 ABSENT (one job). T22 ABSENT (a check from his guide, not reassurance alone). T24 ABSENT: the question is left to the reader, not answered to manufacture suspense. T26 ABSENT (“response” in the heading and “responding” in the line are a callback with a job). T28 and T29 ABSENT (no uplift, no restatement). C01, C03, C04 ABSENT. LINT FINDINGS: D9 accepted: a sentence-for-sentence splice follows the replaced passage's order by construction; T13 and T09 are not happening. E36/E41 accepted: one “you” in 15 words is 6.7 per 100, the same single “you” the replaced sentence has in 18, and the section is direct address throughout. O14 accepted, and this is the one I weighed hardest: “clearer and steadier and less hooked” is the only repeated “and” in the change, and it is a three-item run, which his 2026-10-07 note calls Emulate's trick in a list. I accept it here because it sits in a spoken question put to the reader, where people say a run of outcomes with “and … and”; the same section already runs the same rhythm in the same voice (“sadness or fear or like you’re trying to protect something”); the alternative is the comma triad the source had (“clearer, steadier, and less hooked”), which is the pattern most associated with AI prose; and it occurs once in the change. If the same device shows up in several other places in the article it would become a tic, but nothing in this section's change adds that. No unjustified tell, no added claim, meaning kept.
